title: Asynchronous handshake: slice-based prefetching, kernel hinting, and KV epoch model
content:
Context:
This is a working design note to capture an approach for overlapping prefill and decode work while keeping KV cache correctness, predictable latency for interactive requests, and good throughput for bulk/multiplexed streams. The goal is an implementation that: (a) allows high-priority interactive streams to make forward progress, (b) allows efficient microbatching and kernel selection across heterogeneous requests, and (c) keeps KV cache ownership/consistency cheap and debuggable.

High-level idea summary:
- Break prefill into small 'slices' that can be prefetched asynchronously and later stitched to decode kernels.
- Use an asynchronous handshake protocol between prefill workers and decode workers to advertise readiness, kernel hints, and validity epochs for KV entries.
- Represent KV cache entries with an epoch token and light invalidation metadata so decode can speculatively use cached KV frames and fall back if invalidated.
- Introduce priority lanes (interactive, standard, background) with credit-based backpressure and guaranteed minimal latency for interactive lane.

Why this is different from previous sketches: (notes vs prior files)
- Rather than monolithic prefill batches followed by decode, slices let us interleave smaller prefill work with decode to reduce interactive tail latency.
- The epoch-based KV model focuses on fast local validation (cheap token compare) instead of expensive cache-coordination RPCs during decode.
- Kernel hinting is pushed in-band on the handshake (model variant + quant/profile) so decode kernels can be selected ahead of time and warmed.

Terminology used here:
- slice: a contiguous short block of the input token sequence precomputed into KV frames (e.g., 16-64 tokens).
- prefill-worker: component that consumes incoming request contexts and produces slice-level KV frames.
- decode-worker: component that consumes slices (or live-decoding tokens) and executes autoregressive decode kernels to emit tokens.
- epoch: monotonic generation id attached to KV data indicating its derivation (model version, prompt snapshot, configuration).
- handshake: lightweight async message between prefill and decode workers that contains readiness, slice id, kernel hints, and epoch token.

Design details:
1) Slice boundaries and sizing heuristics
- Default slice size: 32 tokens. Tunable per-customer workload profile.
- Small slices for short prompt + interactive workloads; larger slices used automatically when throughput-favored patterns are detected.
- Heuristic uses: if request contains many short chats or streaming responses, prioritize smaller slices to favor lower latency.

2) Handshake message contents
- slice_id (UUID), request_id, slice_offset, slice_len
- kv_epoch (short string, e.g., model@vX+prompt_sha[:short])
- kernel_hint: {arch, quant_profile, expected_max_seq} encoded as a compact string
- priority_lane: interactive | standard | background
- prefetch_cost_estimate: estimated ms to compute this slice on prefill worker (used by scheduler)
- optional warmup_token: a token that signals decode worker to pre-warm kernels (soft hint)

Note: handshake is intentionally small and optimistic. Decode worker should never block waiting on prefill RPCs during token emit; it can either use a cached slice (kv_epoch match) or request missing slice parts with a bounded timeout fallback.

3) KV epoch model and invalidation
- Each slice's KV frames carry a kv_epoch string. When model variants, tokenizer, or prompt canonicalization changes, prefill assigns a new epoch.
- Decode will accept cached KV frames only if kv_epoch matches the handshake. Local validation is a string compare (cheap).
- Invalidation paths: (a) eager - prefill pushes invalidation token to local KV nodes when epoch rotates, (b) lazy - decode discovers mismatch during handshake and requests updated slice.
- Benefit: avoids RPC-heavy per-token validity checks; mismatch is rare and handled by fallback.

4) Speculative decode and partial emits
- For interactive lane, we allow decode-workers to speculatively emit tokens using partial slice frames. If a later slice invalidates, we log and optionally trigger a correction action (rescore/replace). For most open-source, deterministic model stacks this will be rare.
- Speculative emits are gated by a risk threshold (configurable per-customer).

5) Kernel hinting and warmup
- Prefill handshake includes kernel_hint so decode workers can pick kernels (quantized vs fp16) early. This is important for back-to-back heterogeneous requests where kernel swap cost matters.
- Warmup_token instructs decode worker to pre-allocate kernel memory and resident compiled kernels for expected sequence lengths. Warmup is best-effort.

6) Priority lanes, credits and backpressure
- Three lanes: interactive, standard, background. Each request annotated at admission.
- Scheduler maintains a small credit bucket per lane. Interactive gets reserved credits to ensure sub-50ms tail for short responses. Background can be batched aggressively.
- Credits consumed by prefills and decode tasks; if interactive credits exhausted, we fall back to a lightweight decode-only path (decode without full prefill) to ensure token emit with degraded context.

7) Microbatching strategy across slices
- Within a decode-worker, slices from compatible requests (kernel_hint match + same kv_epoch + same priority lane) can be grouped into microbatches. Microbatched kernels amortize compute for attention and matmuls.
- We use a two-tier grouping: first by kernel_hint/epoch, second by age/latency budget. If we cross latency thresholds, flush smaller microbatches to avoid tail spikes.

8) Failure modes and fallbacks
- Missing slice: decode times out waiting for slice -> fallback to streaming decode without cached KV (full autoreg recompute) or respond with degraded context.
- KV epoch mismatch: request a fresh slice synchronously (bounded ms) and continue. If still failing, degrade gracefully.
- Kernel warmup failed: pick best-effort kernel available. Track metrics to surface frequent mismatches to model-onboarding.

9) Metrics and observability
- Key metrics to emit: handshake latency distribution, slice hit-rate (local KV epoch match), microbatch size distribution, interactive-tail latency (P50/P95/P99), kernel swap rate, speculative-emit rollback rate.
- Tracing spans: admission -> prefill-slice -> handshake -> decode-execute -> emit. Include epoch and kernel_hint in spans for easy debugging.

10) Testing and rollout plan
- Local test harness: synthetic traffic generator with mixed priorities + epoch rotation. Measure correctness and tail latency.
- Canary: route 5% of interactive traffic through new pipeline with epoch logging. Compare decode latency and token correctness to baseline.
- Gradual rollout: increase interactive share only after slice-hit-rate > 98% for stable models.

Open questions / TODOs
- How to encode kernel_hint compactly without tight coupling to runtime internals? (Linnea to propose encoding RFC)
- Should we add a per-slice monotonic counter (sequence number) for partial-replace recovery semantics? (Ravi investigating)
- Decide default slice size per family of tasks (chat vs long-form generation). Need experiment: small slices for < 64 tokens reduces P95 by X? (Diego creating microbench)
- Recovery semantics for speculative emits: immediate rollback vs patch/edited message; product decisions required.

Immediate next steps
- Prototype handshake wire format in the serving-runtime local queue (PR target: #4123).
- Add kv_epoch field to current KV frames and implement cheap string compare-based validation in decode hot path.
- Instrument metrics for handshake latency and slice hit rate.

References / context links:
- Related PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/4123
- Jira: INF-1324 (slice prefetch prototype), INF-1401 (interactive lane budget)
- Slack thread: #serving-runtime - "slice prefetch experiment" (thread ts 1678392)

Notes (informal):
- This is intentionally exploratory. I expect several tradeoffs to change after microbench experiments. The epoch model attempts to minimize coordination cost at the expense of occasional fallback; empirically, most prompt changes that cause epoch rotation are administrative (model update, tokenizer change) and not per-request.
- If we can keep handshake < 1ms on average and slice-hit-rate > 98%, this architecture buys us a lot of flexibility without adding complex cache coherence protocols.

Asha
